rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He prefers the chronology that makes the first revival follow the first death immediately, preserving the sequential force of fa; other chronologies insert a long interval.
rows.anchor: وعلى ما اخترناه تكون الفاء دالة على معناها من التعقيب

rows.speaker: قائل
rows.claim: One interpretation takes the first death as ordinary death and the first revival as resurrection for questioning, using the past tense for a certain future.
rows.anchor: ومن قال: إن الموت الأول: هو المعهود، والإحياء الأول هو للمسألة،

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some infer that there is no punishment in the grave because the verse names two deaths and two lives, with no intervening life after worldly resurrection.
rows.anchor: وقد استدل بهذه الآية قوم على نفي عذاب القبر

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: They reject the disbelievers’ statement about two deaths and lives as proof, since it is their speech and many affirm a pre-worldly life in Adam’s loins.
rows.anchor: قالوا: ولا يجوز أن يستدل بقوله تعالى: ربنا أمتنا اثنتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lack of mention of the questioning life does not establish its absence; alternatively, the second revival may be for questioning, followed by return to God after the resurrection life.
rows.anchor: أنه لا يلزم من عدم ذكر هذه الحياة للمسألة عدمها قبل

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says two deaths describe most people, while some died three times, as in the man who passed a ruined town and Abraham’s birds.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: ذكر الموت مرتين هذا لأكثر الناس،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sequence of giving life, causing death, and reviving proves God’s exclusive power over these acts and establishes resurrection and gathering.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله تعالى: فأحياكم ثم يميتكم ثم يحييكم دليل على اختصاصه تعالى بذلك،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in “then to Him you return” refers to God; an omitted noun means return to His recompense, reward or punishment.
rows.anchor: والظاهر في قوله تعالى: ثم إليه ترجعون أن الهاء عائدة على الله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative takes the pronoun as referring directly to recompense for deeds.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عائدة على الجزاء على الأعمال.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another alternative takes it as the place where God will judge people.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عائدة على الموضع الذي يتولى الله الحكم بينكم فيه.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another alternative refers the pronoun to the revival implied by “He gave you life,” explaining return as renewed helplessness like the beginning of life.
rows.anchor:
وقيل:
عائدة على الإحياء المدلول عليه بقوله: فأحياكم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The corporealists use “to Him you return” to claim God occupies a place, but the wording gives them no proof.
rows.anchor: واستدلت المجسمة بقوله: ثم إليه ترجعون، على أنه تعالى في مكان ولا حجة لهم في ذلك.

rows.speaker: بعض من عاصرناه
rows.claim: A contemporary writer classifies divine names as explicit, pronominal, or implicit, and says Allah is the unique un-derived explicit name for the divine essence.
rows.anchor: قالوا: أسماء الله تعالى على ثلاثة أقسام: مظهرات، ومضمرات، ومستترات.

rows.speaker: بعض من عاصرناه
rows.claim: These writers exalt the pronoun huwa because it points directly to God’s essence, supposedly cuts off attention to anything else, and serves the elite as an invocation.
rows.anchor: اختاره الجلة من المقربين مدارا لذكرهم ومنارا لكل أمرهم فقالوا: يا هو،

rows.speaker: بعض من عاصرناه
rows.claim: They say huwa consists of hāʾ and an added wāw, which drops in the dual and plural, leaving a single letter for the one God.
rows.anchor:
وهو اسم مركب من حرفين وهما:
الهاء والواو،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan finds the discourse about ana, anta, and huwa remote from Arabic grammar and says he has not understood its system.
rows.anchor: ولهم في لفظة أنا وأنت وهو كلام غريب جدا بعيد عما تكلم عليها به أهل اللغة والعربية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in “for you” can denote cause and benefit, ownership or permission, or a broader relation of particularity; the preferred reading is purpose and benefit.
rows.anchor: والأحسن حملها على السبب فيكون مفعولا من أجله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation benefits people religiously through reflection on its design and the afterlife, and materially through food, drink, clothing, marriage, transport, and scenery.
rows.anchor: يحصل الانتفاع الديني والدنيوي

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some use “created for you” to argue that things are presumptively permitted before revealed law.
rows.anchor: وقد استدل بقوله: خلق لكم، من ذهب إلى أن الأشياء قبل ورود الشرع على الإباحة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the lām may mean something other than ownership or permission, this verse alone does not prove the presumption of permissibility.
rows.anchor: وإذا احتمل أن يكون اللام لغير التمليك والإباحة، لم يكن في ذلك دليل

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Others hold that things are forbidden until law permits them, so one should not act without authorization.
rows.anchor: وقد ذهب قوم إلى أن الأشياء قبل ورود الشرع على الحظر

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: A third group suspends judgment because they see arguments for both initial permissibility and prohibition.
rows.anchor: وذهب قوم إلى أن الوقف لنا تعارض عندهم دليل القائلين بالإباحة

rows.speaker: أبو بكر بن فورك عن ابن الصائغ
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sa'igh is reported to say reason has never lacked transmitted guidance: every case has a text, a precedent, or a continuing prior ruling.
rows.anchor: وحكى أبو بكر بن فورك عن ابن الصائغ أنه قال: لم يخل العقل قط من السمع،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “All that is on earth” includes animals, plants, minerals, mountains, and things produced through human crafts and derived processes.
rows.anchor: واندرج تحت قوله: ما في الأرض جميعا، جميع ما كانت الأرض مستقرا له

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some infer that clay is forbidden because the verse grants what is on earth, not the earth itself.
rows.anchor: واستدل بعضهم بذلك على تحريم الطين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Together with the earlier blessing that earth was made a resting place, this verse’s blessing for its contents implies that God made both earth and its contents for people.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم قبل هذا الامتنان بجعل الأرض لنا فراشا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative jamiʿan is a confirmatory circumstantial qualifier of the created things; it means the whole, like kull, not simultaneous existence.
rows.anchor: وانتصب جميعا على الحال من المخلوق، وهي حال مؤكدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taking “what is on earth” to mean the earth and everything in it is distant from the phrase’s literal scope, though it paraphrases its contextual meaning.
rows.anchor: ومن زعم أن المعني بقوله: ما في الأرض، الأرض وما فيها، فهو بعيد عن مدلول اللفظ،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari allows “earth” to mean the lower regions, just as “heaven” can mean the upper regions; the ground and its contents are included below.
rows.anchor: إن أراد بالأرض الجهات السفلية دون الغبراء، كما تذكر السماء، ويراد بها الجهات العلوية، جاز ذلك،

rows.speaker: بعض المنسوبين للحقائق
rows.claim: Some mystical writers read “created for you” as an enumeration of blessings that should prompt gratitude and seeking further gifts.
rows.anchor: خلق لكم ليعد نعمه عليكم، فتقتضي الشكر من نفسك لتطلب المزيد منه.

rows.speaker: أبو عثمان
rows.claim: Abu Uthman says God gave and subjected everything to reveal His generosity, reassure people about the afterlife, and show that great gifts exceed little deeds.
rows.anchor: وهب لك الكل وسخره لك لتستدل به على سعة جوده

rows.speaker: ابن عطاء
rows.claim: Ibn Ata says the whole universe is yours while you are for God; do not let what is yours distract you from Him.
rows.anchor: خلق لكم ليكون الكون كله لك وتكون لله فلا تشتغل بما لك عما أنت له

rows.speaker: بعض البغداديين
rows.claim: Some Baghdadi mystics say blessings make people worship blessings; when a person encounters God, the Benefactor hides the blessings from view.
rows.anchor: أنعم عليك بها، فإن الخلق عبدة النعم لاستيلاء النعم عليهم،

rows.speaker: الثوري
rows.claim: Al-Thawri describes severance from attachments as the highest station of the people of spiritual realization.
rows.anchor: الثوري: أعلى مقامات أهل الحقائق الانقطاع عن العلائق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The particle thumma ordinarily signals temporal delay, although time did not yet exist when the heavens were made.
rows.anchor: والعطف بثم يقتضي التراخي في الزمان، ولا زمان إذ ذاك،

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One explanation makes thumma signal the difference in magnitude between creating earth and creating the heavens, rather than temporal delay.
rows.anchor: فقيل: أشار بثم إلى التفاوت الحاصل بين خلق السماء والأرض في القدر،

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation allows an interval for making mountains, blessing earth, and apportioning its provisions before turning to heaven.
rows.anchor:
وقيل:
لما كان بين خلق الأرض والسماء أعمال من جعل الرواسي والبركة فيها وتقدير الأقوات عطف بثم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word istawā is read with fatḥ by the Hijazis and imāla by Najdis; both forms occur among the seven canonical readers.
rows.anchor: استوى أهل الحجاز على الفتح، ونجد على الإمالة.

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farra interprets istawā ilayh as turning deliberately to create heaven, like an arrow sent straight at its target; al-Zamakhshari chooses this metaphor.
rows.anchor: أقبل وعمد إلى خلقها وقصد من غير أن يريد فيما بين ذلك خلق شيء آخر

rows.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
rows.claim: Al-Rabi ibn Anas interprets istiwāʾ as rising without specifying how or setting limits, understood as the rise of God’s command and authority; al-Tabari prefers it.
rows.anchor: علا وارتفع من غير تكييف ولا تحديد، قاله الربيع بن أنس،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third interpretation takes ilā as ʿalā, meaning God alone held sovereignty over heaven rather than making it the property of creation.
rows.anchor: أن يكون إلى بمعنى على، أي استوى على السماء،

rows.speaker: شاعر
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan introduces a poetic illustration for the reading of istawā as sovereign control over heaven.
rows.anchor: ومن هذا المعنى قول الشاعر

rows.speaker: الحسن البصري
rows.claim: Al-Hasan al-Basri interprets the phrase as God’s command turning toward and settling in heaven; “command” is understood as an omitted noun.
rows.anchor: تحول أمره إلى السماء واستقر فيها، والاستواء هو الاستقرار،

rows.speaker: ابن كيسان
rows.claim: Ibn Kaysan explains it as God’s making and fashioning heaven, a meaning that returns to the first interpretation.
rows.anchor: أن المعنى استوى بخلقه واختراعه إلى السماء، قاله ابن كيسان،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sixth interpretation glosses istawā as completing the work in heaven, but Abu Hayyan says the wording does not support it.
rows.anchor:
السادس:
أن المعنى كمل صنعه فيها، كما تقول: استوى الأمر، وهذا ينبو اللفظ عن الدلالة عليه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A seventh, very remote interpretation makes the pronoun in istawā refer to the smoke, which clashes with the context and pronouns.
rows.anchor: السابع: أن الضمير في استوى عائد على الدخان، وهذا بعيد جدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All these interpretations avoid attributing ordinary movement or change to God, or saying that God enters or is entered by something created.
rows.anchor: وهذه التأويلات كلها فرار عما تقرر في العقول من أن الله تعالى يستحيل أن يتصف بالانتقال المعهود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taswiyah can mean proportioning and straightening the heavens, completing their creation, making them equal, or smoothing their surfaces.
rows.anchor: ومعنى التسوية: تعديل خلقهن وتقويمه وإحلاؤه من العوج والفطور،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The feminine plural pronoun in fasawwāhunna can refer to heaven as a collective noun or to the singular generic “heaven” intended here as plural.
rows.anchor: والضمير في فسواهن عائد على السماء على أنها جمع سماوة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari calls the pronoun ambiguous and treats “seven heavens” as its explanation, comparing it to the construction “he raised him a man.”
rows.anchor: والضمير في فسواهن ضمير مبهم. وسبع سماوات تفسيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan says this is not one of the established Arabic types of indefinite pronouns and weakens the connection to the preceding clause.
rows.anchor: وهذا الذي ذكره الزمخشري ليس واحدا من هذه الضمائر التي سردناها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Making “seven heavens” an apposition to the preceding pronoun is grammatically sound, as in “your brother, I passed by him, Zayd.”
rows.anchor: وقد أعرب بعضهم سبع سموات بدلا من الضمير على أن الضمير عائد على ما قبله، وهو إعراب صحيح،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Parsing “seven heavens” as a direct object with an omitted preposition is poor: سوى does not behave like اختار, and the reading implies more than seven heavens.
rows.anchor: وهذا ليس بجيد من حيث اللفظ ومن حيث المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Parsing it as a second object meaning “made into” is poor because سوى normally takes one object and is not established with the meaning “make.”
rows.anchor: وهذا ليس بجيد، لأن تعدي سوى لواحد هو المعلوم في اللغة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A circumstantial qualifier is also possible, but apposition is stronger because the pronoun refers back to the previous noun.
rows.anchor: والمختار البدل باعتبار عود الضمير على ما قبله والحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scholars disagree whether heaven or earth was created first, each citing the apparent sense of other verses.
rows.anchor: وقد اختلف أهل العلم في أيهما خلق قبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan reads this verse as placing the creation of earthly things before the sevenfold shaping of heaven; earth’s body came first, then it was spread after heaven, reconciling the verses.
rows.anchor: والمختار أن جرم الأرض خلق قبل السماء، وخلقت السماء بعدها، ثم دحيت الأرض بعد خلق السماء،

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some explain the number seven as expressing intensified power and force, since Arabs use seven and seventy for emphatic doubling.
rows.anchor: لأن السبعة والسبعين فيه دلالة على تضاعيف القوة والشدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seven also marks major things in Arab usage: days, heavens, earths, the visible planets, seas, and the gates of Hell.
rows.anchor: والسبعة تذكر في جلائل الأمور: الأيام سبعة، والسموات سبع، والأرض سبع،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hāʾ of huwa and hiya may be made still after wāw, fa, lām, and thumma; it is less common after kāf and interrogative hamza and rare after lakin.
rows.anchor: وتسكين الهاء في هو وهي بعد الواو والفاء واللام وثم جائز

rows.speaker: أبو حمدون
rows.claim: Abu Hamdun has a rare reading with a still hāʾ in “lakin huwa rabbī,” compared to syllable-smoothing in words such as sabʿ and karish.
rows.anchor: وندر بعد لكن، في قراءة أبي حمدون، لكن هو الله ربي،

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو والكسائي وقالون
rows.claim: Abu Amr, al-Kisai, and Qalun read huwa with a still hāʾ; the other readers retain the original vowel, and Yaqub pauses with an added hāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ بتسكين وهو أبو عمرو والكسائي وقالون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “knowing everything,” the intensive form ʿalīm governs “everything”; grammar would ordinarily use a preposition when that complement comes first.
rows.anchor: وكان القياس التعدي باللام حالة التقديم، أو بنفسه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Intensive forms preserve the preposition of verbs that take one; with knowledge or ignorance they use bi-, while other direct-object verbs take li-, resembling the elative.
rows.anchor: إن كان متعديا بحرف جر تعدى المثال بحرف الجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When an intensive form appears to govern a direct object after it, grammarians analyze that object as governed by an omitted verb indicated by the elative.
rows.anchor: أول بأنه معمول لفعل محذوف يدل عليه أفعل التفضيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If “thing” includes both existent and nonexistent entities, this verse directly shows God knows both; if it means only existing things, another proof establishes knowledge of nonexistents.
rows.anchor: فمن أطلقه على الموجود والمعدوم كان تعلق العلم بهما من هذه الآية ظاهرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAlīm is an intensive form, as are ʿālim and ʿallām; Arabs add tāʾ in ʿallāma for emphasis, but that form is not used of God.
rows.anchor: وقد وصف تعالى نفسه بعالم وعليم وعلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine intensification reflects the vast range of known things, not multiple acts of knowledge: God’s single knowledge encompasses every whole and detail, subtle and great, existent and nonexistent.
rows.anchor: لأن علمه تعالى واحد لا تكثير فيه، فلما تعلق علمه تعالى بالجميع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing description “knowing” suits the account of creation and control of the upper and lower worlds, death, and life, all of which display complete knowledge.
rows.anchor: وناسب مقطع هذه الآية بالوصف بمبالغة العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that ʿalīm means knowledge from oneself while ʿālim means knowledge acquired from another is false, since God calls Himself ʿālim without learning.
rows.anchor: وهذا ليس بجيد لأن الله تعالى قد وصف نفسه بالعالم، ولم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The universal wording “knowing everything” rejects the claim that God knows universals but not particulars.
rows.anchor: وفي تعميم قوله تعالى: بكل شيء عليم رد على من زعم أن علم الله تعالى متعلق بالكليات لا بالجزئيات،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine knowledge is one, unchanging, not gained through sense or thought, necessary and unable to cease, never distracted, and encompasses infinitely many objects.
rows.anchor: علم الله تعالى يتميز على علم عباده بكونه واحدا يعلم به جميع المعلومات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’anic parables such as fire, rain, flies, and spiders contain hidden and clear wisdom, eloquence, and apt correspondence; God retains them and praises those who recognize their truth.
rows.anchor: أن ما ضرب به المثل في كتابه: من مستوقد النار، والصيب، والذباب، والعنكبوت،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Parables guide believers and mislead those who reject them; the passage condemns covenant-breakers who sever what must be joined and corrupt the earth, warning that this causes loss.
rows.anchor: وأن في ضربه هدى لمن آمن، وضلالا لمن صد عنه، وذم من نقض عهد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning also tells covenant-breakers that God can revive them after death, gather them, and recompense their deeds, a severe threat.
rows.anchor: والإعلام أن ناقضي عهده هو تعالى قادر على إحيائهم بعد الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After warning comes remembrance of blessings in earth, heaven, and useful creation, joining threat with encouragement as sound-minded moral instruction.
rows.anchor: ثم بعد التخويف ذكرهم تعالى بنعمه التي أنعمها عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The section ends by declaring God’s knowledge encompasses everything from beginning to end.
rows.anchor: ثم ختم ذلك بالفصل الأكبر من إعلامهم بإحاطة علمه بجميع الأشياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waṣiyya means an instruction or covenant delivered with admonition about what should be done.
rows.anchor: الوصية: العهد، وصى بنيه: أي عهد إليهم وتقدم إليهم بما يعمل به مقترنا بوعظ.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Waṣṣā and awṣā are two forms; the doubled form is said to convey greater emphasis or repeated instruction.
rows.anchor: ووصى وأوصى لغتان، إلا أنهم قالوا: إن وصى المشدد يدل على المبالغة والتكثير.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaʿqūb as the prophet’s name is a foreign proper noun and therefore indeclinable; the Arabic word for a male partridge is declinable.
rows.anchor: يعقوب: اسم أعجمي ممنوع الصرف للعلمية والعجمة الشخصية، ويعقوب عربي، وهو ذكر القبج،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The folk explanations that Jacob was named for following his twin or having many descendants fail, since an Arabic derivation would make the name declinable.
rows.anchor: ومن زعم أن يعقوب النبي إنما سمي يعقوب لأنه هو وأخوه العيص توأمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥuḍūr means witnessing or being present; the verb’s kasra form unusually uses a ḍamma imperfect, like a small set of anomalous Arabic verbs.
rows.anchor: الحضور: الشهود، تقول منه: حضر بفتح العين، وفي المضارع: يحضر بضمها،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Isḥāq as a name is a foreign proper noun and indeclinable, while the verbal noun from asḥaq would be declinable if used as a name.
rows.anchor: إسحاق: اسم أعجمي لا ينصرف للعلمية والعجمة الشخصية، وإسحاق: مصدر أسحق،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grammarians offer several broken plurals for Ishaq, Jacob, and Israel; Kufans propose forms such as asāḥiq and yaʿāqiba.
rows.anchor: وقالوا في الجمع: أساحقة وأساحيق، وفي جمع يعقوب: يعاقبة ويعاقيب،

rows.speaker: أبو العباس
rows.claim: Abu al-Abbas rejects Kufan plurals that drop the hamza, arguing it is not an augment; he allows forms like abārih and asāmīʿ and recommends sound plurals.
rows.anchor: رد أبو العباس على من أسقط الهمزة، لأن هذا ليس موضع زيادتها.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥanaf denotes inclination; al-Aḥnaf was named for a deviation between his feet, as a cited poem confirms.
rows.anchor: الحنف: لغة الميل، وبه سمي الأحنف لميل كان في إحدى قدميه

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba defines ḥanaf as uprightness and says al-Aḥnaf was named optimistically, like calling a bitten person “safe.”
rows.anchor: وقال ابن قتيبة: الحنف الاستقامة، وسمي الأحنف على سبيل التفاؤل،

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffal says ḥanīf is a label for a follower of Islam, like the names of other religions.
rows.anchor: وقال القفال: الحنف لقب لمن دان بالإسلام كسائر ألقاب الديانات.

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Umar’s verse thanks God for guiding his heart to Islam and the ḥanīf religion.
rows.anchor:
عمر:
حمدت الله حين هدى فؤادي

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj defines ḥanīf as turning away from the common way toward the path one has adopted, and cites a poem.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: الحنيف: المائل عما عليه العامة إلى ما لزمه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The asbāṭ are Jacob’s twelve sons and their descendant tribes, parallel to Ishmael’s tribes; the term suggests a continuing succession.
rows.anchor: الأسباط: جمع سبط، وهم في بني إسرائيل كالقبائل في بني إسماعيل،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other etymologies derive sibṭ from spreading or branching: successive giving, a reversal of basṭ, or a tree with tangled branches; it also came to mean a grandson.
rows.anchor:
وقيل:
أصل الأسباط من السبط، وهو الشجر الملتف، والسبط: الجماعة الراجعون إلى أصل واحد.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and al-Husayn are called the Prophet’s two sibṭs because of their numerous descendants; the term later extended to a daughter’s son and descendants.
rows.anchor: ويقال للحسن والحسين: سبطا رسول الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shiqqāq is the verbal noun of shāqq and means hostility or opposition, as each side stands on a different side; a poem illustrates the division.
rows.anchor: الشقاق: مصدر شاقه، كما تقول: ضارب ضرابا، وخالف خلافا، ومعناه: المعاداة والمخالفة،

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another derivation connects shiqqāq with hardship because each opponent seeks to burden the other.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو من المشقة، لأن كل واحد منهما يحرص على ما يشق على صاحبه.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kifāya means sufficiency: “kafānī” means that something sufficed or made one independent, as shown by a cited poem.
rows.anchor: الكفاية: الإحساب. كفاني كذا: أي أحسبني،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣibgha is the form or state produced by dye; ṣibgh can mean the dye itself, the act of dyeing, or a change to a color, with reported vowel variants in its imperfect.
rows.anchor: الصبغة: فعلة من صبغ، كالجلسة من جلس، وأصلها الهيئة التي يقع عليها الصبغ.

rows.speaker: نافع وابن عامر
rows.claim: Nafi and Ibn Amir read awṣā, while the other readers read waṣṣā; Thalab transmits differences between the Medinan and Iraqi codices.
rows.anchor: قرأ نافع وابن عامر: وأوصى، وقرأ الباقون: ووصى.

rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: Thalab lists twelve Medinan–Iraqi written/read variants: sārʿū, yaqūl, yartadd, alladhīna ittakhadhū, khayran minhumā/minhā, fatawakkal/tawakkal, an/yuzhir, bimā/fīmā kasabat, tashtahī/tashtahī, al-ghaniyy/huwa al-ghaniyy, and yakhāf/falā yakhāf.
rows.anchor: اختلف مصحف أهل المدينة وأهل العراق في اثني عشر حرفا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari and al-Mahdawi take “by it” to refer to Abraham’s religion, explicitly mentioned nearby.
rows.anchor: وبها متعلق بأوصى، والضمير عائد على الملة في قوله: ومن يرغب عن ملة إبراهيم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya initially prefers “the word” that Abraham declared, “I submit to the Lord of the worlds,” because it is the nearest antecedent.
rows.anchor: ابتدأ ابن عطية وقال: هو أصوب، لأنه أقرب مذكور،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan prefers “the religion” as antecedent because it is explicit and broader than the word, encompassing what most secures success in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: ورجح العود على الملة بأنه يكون المفسر مصرحا به

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other proposed antecedents for “by it” are the later command to die only as Muslims, the unmentioned but implied confession of faith, the testament itself, or obedience.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يعود على الكلمة المتأخرة، وهو قوله: فلا تموتن إلا وأنتم مسلمون.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham’s sons included Ishmael by Hagar and Isaac by Sarah, plus six sons by Qatura; only Ishmael and Isaac left enduring lines.
rows.anchor: هؤلاء الثمانية ولده لصلبه، والعقب الباقي فيهم اثنان إسماعيل وإسحاق لا غير.

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: Most readers put Yaʿqūb in the nominative, either coordinating him with Abraham as another who instructed his sons, or making him a subject with an omitted predicate; coordination is clearer.
rows.anchor: قرأ الجمهور: ويعقوب بالرفع، وقرأ إسماعيل

rows.speaker: إسماعيل بن عبد الله المكي والضرير وعمرو بن فائد الأسواري
rows.claim: These readers put Yaʿqūb in the accusative, coordinating him with “his sons” and taking them as Jacob’s grandsons, since Jacob was Isaac’s son.
rows.anchor: وقرأ إسماعيل بن عبد الله المكي، والضرير، وعمرو بن فائد الأسواري: بالنصب.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Abraham speaks the “O my sons” address, grammarians differ whether an unspoken verb of saying is needed; Kufans treat testament as speech itself.
rows.anchor: وعند الكوفيين لا يحتاج إلى ذلك، لأن الوصية في معنى القول،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling them “my sons” is tender and encourages acceptance, stirring them toward Islam; the statement that God chose the religion makes departure from it irrational.
rows.anchor: وكون النداء بلفظ البنين مضافين إليه تلطف غريب وترجئة للقبول

rows.speaker: أبي وعبد الله والضحاك
rows.claim: Ubayy, Abdullah, and al-Dahhak read “an yā banayya”; an is explanatory, while grammarians who reject that use call it redundant.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي وعبد الله والضحاك: أن يا بني،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “God chose the religion for you” means He selected Islam as the purest religion known to them.
rows.anchor: إن الله اصطفى لكم الدين، أي استخلصه لكم وتخيره لكم صفوة الأديان.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Do not die except as Muslims” means remain in Islam; the apparent ban on dying actually bans being in a state other than Islam.
rows.anchor: هذا استثناء من الأحوال، أي إلا على هذه الحالة، والمعنى: الثبوت على الإسلام،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrasing is concise admonition: because death is certain but its time unknown, the command keeps people mindful and continually in the state in which they should meet death.
rows.anchor: وقد تضمن هذا الكلام إيجازا بليغا ووعظا وتذكيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command also forbids actions that could cause a person to meet death outside Islam, like “do not let me see you here” really meaning leave the place.
rows.anchor: وهذا على الحقيقة نهي عن تعاطي الأشياء التي تكون سببا للموافاة على غير الإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “do not let me see you here,” the speaker does not ban seeing itself but the listener’s presence that would cause it; the phrasing conveys anger and aversion.
rows.anchor: لا أرينك هاهنا، لا ينهى نفسه عن الرؤية، ولكن المعنى على النهي عن حضوره في هذا المكان،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The testament shows Abraham’s concern for religion even though his sons already followed Islam, and that he sought their safety in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: ففي ذلك ما كان عليه إبراهيم من الاهتمام بأمر الدين، حتى وصى به من كان ملتبسا به،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He addressed all his sons, without exception, and left the testament unrestricted by time or place, then ended with the strongest warning against dying outside Islam.
rows.anchor: ومنها أنه عمم بنيه، ولم يخص أحدا منهم،

rows.speaker: رسول الله عن النعمان بن بشير
rows.claim: The Prophet challenged al-Nuʿman’s father over a gift to one child, asking whether he wanted equal dutifulness among them and refusing to witness injustice.
rows.anchor: حين نحله أبوه شيئا، فقال له رسول الله

rows.speaker: المؤرخون
rows.claim: Historians say Ishmael was taken to Mecca as an infant, was fourteen years older than Isaac, and was eighty-nine when Abraham died; Isaac lived 180 years and was buried beside Abraham.
rows.anchor:
قال المؤرخون:
نقل إبراهيم ولده إسماعيل إلى مكة وهو رضيع،

rows.speaker: المؤرخون
rows.claim: Historians place about 2,600 years between Abraham’s death and Muhammad’s birth, while Jewish chronology subtracts about 400 years.
rows.anchor: وكان بين وفاة أبيه إبراهيم ومولد محمد

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says the verse was revealed about Jews who claimed Jacob prescribed Judaism: on reaching Egypt, Jacob saw idol and celestial worship and asked his sons what they would worship after him.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: لما دخل يعقوب مصر رآهم يعبدون الأوثان والنيرين،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation informs the Prophet of Jacob’s actual testament and refutes the Jewish claim that he died a Jew.
rows.anchor: فأنزل الله هذه الآية إعلاما لنبيه بما وصى به يعقوب، وتكذيبا لليهود.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most grammarians take disjunctive am as “rather, were you witnesses?”; it shifts topic without canceling the preceding statement and rebukes the audience by implying they were not witnesses.
rows.anchor: أنها هنا منقطعة بمعنى بل والهمزة.

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another reading takes am as “rather,” saying the audience—or their ancestors whose reports they inherited—were witnesses, thereby challenging the Jewish attribution of Judaism to Jacob.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أم هنا بمعنى: بل، والمعنى بل كنتم، أي كان أسلافكم،

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya reads it as a reproachful question: did you witness Jacob’s testament and claim knowledge, when in fact you did not and are inventing the claim?
rows.anchor: قال لهم على جهة التقرير والتوبيخ أشهدتم يعقوب وعلمتم بما أوصى

rows.speaker: بعض النحويين
rows.claim: A Yemeni dialect reportedly permits am to mean the interrogative hamza at the start of a sentence; Abu Hayyan has not found this in grammarians.
rows.anchor: وأم تكون بمعنى ألف الاستفهام في صدر الكلام لغة يمانية

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari says am can introduce a question mid-sentence after an earlier clause, as in “or do they say he invented it?”
rows.anchor:
وحكى الطبري أن أم يستفهم بها في وسط
كلام قد تقدم صدره،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan summarizes three analyses: the common disjunctive “rather + hamza,” “rather” alone, or interrogative hamza alone.
rows.anchor: وتلخص أن أم هنا فيها ثلاثة أقوال

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says the address could be to believers, who know the event by revelation, or to Jews claiming prophets died Jews; he prefers a connected alternative asking whether they accuse prophets or witnessed Jacob’s insistence on monotheism.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: الخطاب للمؤمنين بمعنى: ما شاهدتم ذلك، وإنما حصل لكم العلم به من طريق الوحي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects al-Zamakhshari’s connected am because it requires deleting the first alternative clause, a deletion unattested in Arabic and turning one question into an incomplete clause.
rows.anchor: ولا نعلم أحدا أجاز حذف هذه الجملة، ولا يحفظ ذلك، لا في شعر ولا غيره،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic can omit a preceding coordinated phrase with wāw or fa when context supplies it, and rarely with aw or ḥattā; this does not establish omission before connected am.
rows.anchor: وإما يحذف المعطوف عليه ويبقى المعطوف مع الواو والفاء، إذا دل على ذلك دليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poet omits the second alternative after connected am (“was her seeking right-guided or not?”) because a positive question entails its negative opposite; other paired contrasts may likewise be omitted.
rows.anchor:
فما أدري أرشد طلابها
يريد: أم غير رشد، فحذف لدلالة الكلام عليه،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first idh makes “when Jacob was present” an adverbial of the witnesses’ presence, not an object; “death came” means its causes approached, since a dying person cannot speak.
rows.anchor: إذ حضر العامل في إذ شهداء، وذلك على جهة الظرف، لا على جهة المفعول،

rows.speaker: شاعر
rows.claim: A cited poet has a speaker tell people to seek an excuse because “I am death,” illustrating death as approaching causes rather than the instant of dying.
rows.anchor: وقل لهم بادروا العذر والتمسوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression that death “comes” is a strange euphemism: death is absent but must arrive; a prayer calls death the best absent thing awaited.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله: حضر، كناية غريبة، إنه غائب لا بد أن يقدم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading ḥaḍira with kasra is a dialect form; its imperfect with ḍamma is anomalous, and the object is advanced before the subject for emphasis.
rows.anchor: وقرىء: حضر بكسر الضاد، وقد ذكرنا أن ذلك لغة،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second idh (“when he said to his sons”) substitutes for the first; grammarians differ whether the first governor is repeated or the same governor applies.
rows.anchor:
إذ:
بدل من إذ في قوله: إذ حضر، فالعامل فيه إما شهداء

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffal treats the second idh as the time of Jacob’s presence, governed by ḥaḍara, effectively making both adverbials refer to one time.
rows.anchor: وزعم القفال أن إذ وقت للحضور، فالعامل فيه حضر،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mā is a complete interrogative noun for what is worshipped, grammatically the direct object of the following verb.
rows.anchor: ما: استفهام عما لا يعقل، وهو اسم تام منصوب بالفعل بعده.

rows.speaker: قائل
rows.claim: If mā can denote both rational and nonrational beings, Jacob’s question can include humans, angels, celestial bodies, and idols.
rows.anchor: قول من زعم أن ما مبهمة في كل شيء، يكون هنا يقع على من يعقل وما لا يعقل،

rows.speaker: قائل
rows.claim: If mā is restricted to nonrational things, it can ask about the nature of an object, as in “What is Zayd, a jurist or a poet?”
rows.anchor: فقيل: هو سؤال عن صفة المعبود، لأن ما يسأل بها عن الصفات

rows.speaker: قائل
rows.claim: Another explanation is that familiar objects of worship then were inanimate, so the sons understood the question and answered that they worship none of them.
rows.anchor: وقيل: سأل بما لأن المعبودات المتعارفة في ذلك الوقت كانت جمادات،

rows.speaker: قائل
rows.claim: One says Jacob used mā instead of man to test his sons and avoid giving them a hint toward a particular person or faith.
rows.anchor:
وقيل:
استفهم بما عن المعبود تجربة لهم، ولم يقل من لئلا يطرق لهم الاهتداء،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plain sense asks what they will worship; al-Qaffal instead says Jacob urged them to seek only God’s face and feared worldly distraction rather than idol worship.
rows.anchor:
وظاهر الكلام أنه استفهم عن الذي يعبدون، أي
العبادة المشروعة؟

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob’s question shows the prophets’ concern for their children was focused on religion.
rows.anchor: وفي ذلك دليل على أن شفقة الأنبياء عليهم الصلاة والسلام على أولادهم كانت في باب الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “After me” means after Jacob’s death.
rows.anchor: من بعدي: يريد من بعد موتي،

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: It is reported that Jacob, when prophets were offered a choice, chose death but asked first for time to advise his family and sons.
rows.anchor: وحكي أن يعقوب عليه السلام حين خير، كما يخير الأنبياء، اختار الموت

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: The majority read “your fathers Abraham, Ishmael, and Isaac”; Abraham onward can be apposition or clarification of “your fathers,” with an omitted “I mean” also possible.
rows.anchor: قالوا نعبد إلهك وإله آبائك إبراهيم وإسماعيل وإسحاق: هذه قراءة الجمهور.

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy’s reading omits “your fathers,” giving “and the God of Abraham.”
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي: وإله إبراهيم، بإسقاط آبائك.

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والحسن وابن يعمر والجحدري وأبو رجاء
rows.claim: These readers have the singular “your father”; Abraham then clarifies or stands in apposition to it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس، والحسن، وابن يعمر، والجحدري، وأبو رجاء: وإله أبيك.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling Abraham and what follows “your fathers” shows that an uncle can be called a father and that a grandfather is also called a father.
rows.anchor: وفيه دلالة على أن العم يطلق عليه أب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas uses these verses and Jacob’s “fathers” in 12:38 to argue that a grandfather inherits as a father when the father is absent, excluding siblings.
rows.anchor: وقد استدل ابن عباس بذلك وبقوله: واتبعت ملة آبائي إبراهيم وإسحاق ويعقوب

rows.speaker: الصديق وجماعة من الصحابة وأبو حنيفة
rows.claim: Abu Bakr, a group of Companions, and Abu Hanifa treat the grandfather as the father in inheritance when no father survives.
rows.anchor: وهو مذهب الصديق وجماعة من الصحابة، رضوان الله عليهم أجمعين، وهو قول أبي حنيفة.

rows.speaker: زيد بن ثابت ومالك وأبو يوسف والشافعي
rows.claim: Zayd ibn Thabit, Malik, Abu Yusuf, and al-Shafiʿi treat the grandfather like siblings, guaranteeing him a third if division would reduce his share below that.
rows.anchor: وقال زيد بن ثابت: هو بمنزلة الإخوة، ما لم تنقصه المقاسمة من الثلث،

rows.speaker: علي وابن أبي ليلى
rows.claim: Ali and Ibn Abi Layla treat the grandfather as one sibling, guaranteeing him a sixth if division would reduce his share below that.
rows.anchor: وقال علي: هو بمنزلة أحد الإخوة، ما لم تنقصه المقاسمة من السدس،

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh records أبين as an inflected plural of father, allowing “your father” to be construed as a plural with its nūn dropped in annexation.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو جمع سقطت منه النون للإضافة، فقد جمع أب على أبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sons repeat the verb “we worship” instead of merely saying “your god,” explicitly matching their answer to Jacob’s question.
rows.anchor: وفي إجابتهم له بإظهار الفعل تأكيد لما أجابوه به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling God “your god” and “the god of your fathers” emphasizes that questioner and respondents share one deity.
rows.anchor: وإضافة الإله إلى يعقوب فيه دليل على اتحاد معبود السائل والمجيب لفظا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating “and the god” before a genitive pronoun follows the usual rule that a conjunction on such a pronoun repeats its preposition; omitting it with an explicit noun would better signal unity.
rows.anchor: وإنما كرر لفظ وإله، لأنه لا يصح العطف على الضمير المجرور إلا بإعادة جاره،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jacob is named first because he asked, Abraham because he is the origin, and Ishmael before Isaac because he was older or honored as the Prophet’s ancestor.
rows.anchor: وبدأ أولا بإضافة الإله إلى يعقوب، لأنه هو السائل، وقدم إبراهيم، لأنه الأصل،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only these ancestors are named because they were the best people of their eras; the answer does not enumerate every being people worshipped.
rows.anchor: واقتصر على هؤلاء، لأنهم كانوا خير الناس في أزمانهم، ولم يعم،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “One God” can be an apposition or a circumstantial qualifier; either makes explicit that one shared deity is a single individual, not several.
rows.anchor: هذه الحال، أو البدل، هو التنصيص على أن معبودهم واحد فرد،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari parses “one God” as specification, but grammarians disallow specification with an indefinite or ambiguous noun.
rows.anchor: وجوز الزمخشري أن ينتصب على الاختصاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We submit to Him” is best read as a second coordinated part of the answer: worship is recurring action, while the nominal “submitting” expresses their permanent surrender.
rows.anchor: والأول أبلغ، وهو أن تكون الجملة معطوفة على قوله: نعبد،

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari calls the clause parenthetical and explanatory; Abu Hayyan rejects this because it is not inserted between tightly linked parts of one speaker’s statement.
rows.anchor: وأجاز الزمخشري أن تكون جملة اعتراضية مؤكدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A parenthetical clause strengthens a relation between parts that belong together, such as a relative clause and antecedent or a condition and result; “we submit to Him” is not such an insertion.
rows.anchor: والذي ذكره النحويون أن جملة الاعتراض هي الجملة التي تفيد تقوية بين جزأي موصول وصلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sons’ statement is complete before “we submit,” and God’s statement follows it, so it cannot be a parenthesis inserted by the same speaker between linked parts.
rows.anchor: لأن قبلها كلاما مستقلا، وبعدها كلام مستقل،

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya reads “we submit to Him” as a nominal clause meaning “we were and will be so,” or possibly as a circumstantial clause; he says the first is more laudatory.
rows.anchor:
ابن عطية: ونحن له مسلمون ابتداء وخبر، أي:
كذلك كنا ونحن نكون.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: There is no need to supply Ibn Atiyya’s omitted “thus we were”; the clause can coordinate directly with “we worship,” which is preferable to ellipsis.
rows.anchor: ومتى أمكن حمل الكلام على غير إضمار، مع صحة المعنى، كان أولى

rows.speaker: المقلدة
rows.claim: Traditionalists use the sons’ answer as proof that imitation suffices: Jacob’s sons name the deity worshipped by their ancestors, and Jacob does not object.
rows.anchor: تمسك بهذه الآية المقلدة، وقالوا: إن أبناء يعقوب اكتفوا بالتقليد،

rows.speaker: التعليمية
rows.claim: The Talimiyya argue that God is known only by instruction from a prophet or imam, since the sons appeal to the deity worshipped by Jacob and earlier fathers.
rows.anchor:
واستدل بها التعليمية، قالوا:
لا طريق لمعرفة الله تعالى إلا بتعليم الرسول والإمام،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse only records their confession of worship; it does not establish that their belief arose from imitation or instruction.
rows.anchor: لأن الآية لم تتضمن إلا الإقرار بعبادة الإله

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A report addressed to Banu Hashim and Fatima warns that family lineage cannot substitute for one’s deeds or protect one from God.
rows.anchor: وروي: يا بني هاشم! لا يأتيني الناس بأعمالهم وتأتوني بأنسابكم!

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn Atiyya says this verse refutes the determinists who deny that a servant acquires or performs acts.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: وفي هذه الآية رد على الجبرية القائلين: لا اكتساب للعبد.

rows.speaker: الجبرية
rows.claim: The Jabriyya say people are compelled in their acts, have no choice, and relate to action like a branch moved by an external force.
rows.anchor: قول الجبرية، وهو أن العبد مجبور على فعله، وأنه لا اختيار له في ذلك،

rows.speaker: القدرية
rows.claim: The Qadariyya deny compulsion and say people possess power to bring their acts into existence.
rows.anchor: قول القدرية، وهو أنهم ليسوا مجبورين على الفعل، بل لهم قدرة على إيجاد الفعل.

rows.speaker: المعتزلة
rows.claim: The Muʿtazila say God creates a person’s capacity before the act, leaving the person able either to perform or omit it.
rows.anchor: قول المعتزلة، أن العبد له قدرة يخلقها الله له قبل الفعل،

rows.speaker: أهل السنة والجماعة
rows.claim: The Sunni position is that God creates capacity and empowerment alongside the act; a person performs good or evil without compulsion, and this grounds reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: مذهب أهل السنة والجماعة: أن الله يخلق للعبد تمكينا وقدرة مع الفعل

rows.speaker: أبو الحسن
rows.claim: Abu al-Hasan says created capacity relates to an act without causing it; God creates both, and the servant’s acquisition is that act’s relation to his capacity.
rows.anchor: قول أبي الحسن: أن القدرة صفة متعلقة بالمقدور من غير تأثير في المقدور،

rows.speaker: الباقلاني
rows.claim: Al-Baqillani says the act itself is not intrinsically obedience or sin; its quality as such arises through the created capacity.
rows.anchor: قول الباقلاني: أن ذات الفعل لم تحصل له صفة، كونه طاعة ومعصية،

rows.speaker: أبو إسحاق الأسفرائيني
rows.claim: Abu Ishaq al-Isfarayini says the eternal and created capacities both relate to the act, so the servant’s act occurs through divine assistance.
rows.anchor: أن القدرتين، القديمة والحديثة، إذا تعلقتا بمقدور وقع بهما،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each person is accountable only for their own earnings; no one benefits from another’s good deeds or bears another’s sins, as 6:164 and the proverb say.
rows.anchor: ولا تسئلون عما كانوا يعملون: جملة توكيدية لما قبلها،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument can expose an opponent by applying a premise they accept, even when it is not the substantive proof; the Prophet’s actual proof of his mission was miracles.
rows.anchor: للإنسان أن يحتج على غيره بما يجري مجرى المناقضة لقوله،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once opponents remained defiant after proof, the argument meets them on their own hereditary view: if religion follows ancestors, the common ancestor’s faith is the better claim.
rows.anchor: فقال: إن كان الدين بالاتباع، فالمتفق عليه أولى.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because each person bears only their own deeds, the verse disproves punishing children of polytheists for their parents’ sins.
rows.anchor: وفي قوله: لها ما كسبت إلى آخره، دلالة على بطلان قول من يقول بجواز تعذيب أولاد المشركين بذنوب آبائهم.

rows.speaker: السجاوندي
rows.claim: Al-Sajawandi analyzes ḥanīfan as an accusative of cut-off, estimating “we follow”; this is a Kufan parse, which Basrans reject.
rows.anchor: وتقدير الفعل نتبع حنيفا، وأنه منصوب على القطع، حكاه السجاوندي،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An implied verb is a straightforward analysis; ḥanīfan may also be a circumstantial qualifier of the annexed noun, though Abu Hayyan rejects such a qualifier when the possessor’s governor does not govern it.
rows.anchor: وأما إضمار الفعل فهو قريب، ويمكن أن يكون منصوبا على الحال من المضاف،

rows.speaker: هبة الله بن الشجري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Shajari prefers taking ḥanīfan as a circumstantial qualifier of milla despite masculine agreement, because milla means the masculine noun dīn.
rows.anchor: وأوجه من ذلك عندي أن يجعله حالا من الملة، وإن خالفها بالتذكير،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether qualifying Abraham or his religion, ḥanīfan is an inseparable state because Abraham’s religion and Abraham himself never departed from upright monotheism.
rows.anchor: وتكون حالا لازمة، لأن دين إبراهيم لم ينفك عن الحنيفية،

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas defines ḥanīf as one who inclines away from all other religions.
rows.anchor: والحنيف: هو المائل عن الأديان كلها، قاله ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj defines ḥanīf as one who turns away from the common religion toward the chosen path, or as upright.
rows.anchor: المائل عما عليه العامة، قاله الزجاج، أو المستقيم، قاله ابن قتيبة

rows.speaker: ابن قتيبة
rows.claim: Ibn Qutayba defines ḥanīf as upright.
rows.anchor: أو المستقيم، قاله ابن قتيبة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وابن الحنفية
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Hanafiyya also define ḥanīf as a pilgrim.
rows.anchor: أو الحاج، قاله ابن عباس أيضا وابن الحنفية،

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid defines ḥanīf as a follower.
rows.anchor: أو الحاج، قاله ابن عباس أيضا وابن الحنفية، أو المتبع، قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi defines ḥanīf as sincere and devoted.
rows.anchor: أو المخلص، قاله السدي أو المخالف للكل، قاله ابن بحر

rows.speaker: ابن بحر
rows.claim: Ibn Bahr defines ḥanīf as one who differs from everyone else.
rows.anchor: أو المخالف للكل، قاله ابن بحر

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak defines ḥanīf as Muslim; when “ḥanīf” is paired with “Muslim,” he says it means pilgrim.
rows.anchor: أو المسلم، قاله الضحاك، قال: فإذا جمع الحنيف مع المسلم فهو الحاج،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other related definitions connect ḥanīf with circumcision, pilgrimage rites, and avoiding marriage to close female relatives.
rows.anchor: أو المختتن. أو الحنف: هو الاختتان، وإقامة المناسك،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham alone is singled out because God made him an exemplar for instituting pilgrimage rites, circumcision, and other Islamic practices followed until the end of time.
rows.anchor: لأن الله اختص إبراهيم بالإمامة، لما سنه من مناسك الحج والختان،

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥanīf became a marker distinguishing believers from disbelievers: Abraham’s followers were called ḥanīfs, while those leaving his religion were named after other religions.
rows.anchor: وصارت الحنيفية علما مميزا بين المؤمن والكافر
